claim: Human BJ iPSC-derived NPCs showed homogeneous expression of the NPC markers Nestin and Sox2.
source: Human BJ iPSC-derived NPCs showed homogeneous expression of the NPC markers Nestin and Sox2.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: After 3 weeks of differentiation, a majority (~85%) of cells expressed the neuronal marker MAP2.
source: After 3 weeks of differentiation, a majority (~85%) of cells expressed the neuronal marker MAP2 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Neurons after ~4 weeks could be induced to fire multiple action potentials.
source: Consistent with a previous study (Johnson et al., 2007), neurons after ~4 weeks could be induced to fire multiple action potentials (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and cited reference.

claim: The loss of hexokinase (HK2) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDHA) expression marks the transition from aerobic glycolysis in neural progenitor cells (NPC) to neuronal oxidative phosphorylation.
source: We found that the loss of hexokinase (HK2) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDHA) expression, together with a switch in pyruvate kinase gene splicing from PKM2 to PKM1, marks the transition from aerobic glycolysis in neural progenitor cells (NPC) to neuronal oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and protein expression data showing dramatic decreases in HK2 and LDHA during neuronal differentiation.

claim: A switch in pyruvate kinase gene splicing from PKM2 to PKM1 marks the transition from aerobic glycolysis in neural progenitor cells (NPC) to neuronal oxidative phosphorylation.
source: We found that the loss of hexokinase (HK2) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDHA) expression, together with a switch in pyruvate kinase gene splicing from PKM2 to PKM1, marks the transition from aerobic glycolysis in neural progenitor cells (NPC) to neuronal oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and RT-PCR validation showing PKM2 expression in NPCs and PKM1 expression in neurons.

claim: The protein levels of c-MYC and N-MYC, transcriptional activators of the HK2 and LDHA genes, decrease dramatically during neuronal differentiation.
source: The protein levels of c-MYC and N-MYC, transcriptional activators of the HK2 and LDHA genes, decrease dramatically.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data showing ~70% and ~85% decreases in c-MYC and N-MYC protein levels, respectively.

claim: Constitutive expression of HK2 and LDHA during differentiation leads to neuronal cell death.
source: Constitutive expression of HK2 and LDHA during differentiation leads to neuronal cell death, indicating that the shut-off aerobic glycolysis is essential for neuronal survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ~40% condensed nuclei in neuronal cultures from NPCs constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA compared to ~6% in control.

claim: The shut-off of aerobic glycolysis is essential for neuronal survival.
source: Constitutive expression of HK2 and LDHA during differentiation leads to neuronal cell death, indicating that the shut-off aerobic glycolysis is essential for neuronal survival.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that constitutive HK2 and LDHA expression causes neuronal death.

claim: The metabolic regulators PGC-1α and ERRγ increase significantly upon neuronal differentiation.
source: The metabolic regulators PGC-1α and ERRγ increase significantly upon neuronal differentiation to sustain the transcription of metabolic and mitochondrial genes, whose levels are unchanged compared to NPCs, revealing distinct transcriptional regulation of metabolic genes in the proliferation and post-mitotic differentiation states.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and immunoblotting data showing ~3-4 fold increases in PGC-1α and ~2.8-3.4 fold increases in ERRγ.

claim: PGC-1α and ERRγ sustain the transcription of metabolic and mitochondrial genes during neuronal differentiation.
source: The metabolic regulators PGC-1α and ERRγ increase significantly upon neuronal differentiation to sustain the transcription of metabolic and mitochondrial genes, whose levels are unchanged compared to NPCs, revealing distinct transcriptional regulation of metabolic genes in the proliferation and post-mitotic differentiation states.
evidence: Supported by knockdown experiments showing decreased expression of TCA and mitochondrial genes when PGC-1α or ERRγ are depleted.

claim: The levels of metabolic and mitochondrial genes are unchanged in neurons compared to NPCs.
source: The metabolic regulators PGC-1α and ERRγ increase significantly upon neuronal differentiation to sustain the transcription of metabolic and mitochondrial genes, whose levels are unchanged compared to NPCs, revealing distinct transcriptional regulation of metabolic genes in the proliferation and post-mitotic differentiation states.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing no significant changes in TCA and mitochondrial respiratory complex gene expression.

claim: There is distinct transcriptional regulation of metabolic genes in the proliferation and post-mitotic differentiation states.
source: The metabolic regulators PGC-1α and ERRγ increase significantly upon neuronal differentiation to sustain the transcription of metabolic and mitochondrial genes, whose levels are unchanged compared to NPCs, revealing distinct transcriptional regulation of metabolic genes in the proliferation and post-mitotic differentiation states.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that metabolic gene expression is maintained at similar levels but through different transcriptional regulators (MYC/E2F in NPCs vs. PGC-1α/ERRγ in neurons).

claim: Mitochondrial mass increases proportionally with neuronal mass growth.
source: Mitochondrial mass increases proportionally with neuronal mass growth, indicating an unknown mechanism linking mitochondrial biogenesis to cell size.
evidence: Supported by data showing ~4-fold increase in both mtDNA copy number and protein mass in 3-week neurons compared to NPCs.

claim: There is an unknown mechanism linking mitochondrial biogenesis to cell size.
source: Mitochondrial mass increases proportionally with neuronal mass growth, indicating an unknown mechanism linking mitochondrial biogenesis to cell size.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the observed proportional relationship between mitochondrial mass and cell size.

claim: Neurons rely on oxidative phosphorylation to meet energy demands.
source: Neurons rely on oxidative phosphorylation to meet energy demands.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Malfunctions of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) lead to a wide range of neurological disorders.
source: Malfunctions of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) lead to a wide range of neurological disorders, and are frequently observed in neurodegenerative diseases (Lin and Beal, 2006; Schon and Przedborski, 2011; Koopman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Chronic exposure of the brain to the lipophilic pesticide rotenone causes dopaminergic neuron degeneration.
source: For example, chronic exposure of the brain to the lipophilic pesticide rotenone causes dopaminergic neuron degeneration (Betarbet et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Hereditary mutations in OXPHOS genes cause Leigh syndrome, a severe early childhood neurodegeneration.
source: Hereditary mutations in OXPHOS genes cause Leigh syndrome, a severe early childhood neurodegeneration (Finsterer, 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Expression of the majority of glycolysis genes was decreased in neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 1G, expression of the majority of glycolysis genes was decreased in neurons, particularly enzymes acting at the steps after fructose 1,6 phosphate formation, i.e., ALDOA to LDHA/B, which declined to half to one-third of their level in NPCs.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Enzymes acting at the steps after fructose 1,6 phosphate formation (ALDOA to LDHA/B) declined to half to one-third of their level in NPCs.
source: As shown in Figure 1G, expression of the majority of glycolysis genes was decreased in neurons, particularly enzymes acting at the steps after fructose 1,6 phosphate formation, i.e., ALDOA to LDHA/B, which declined to half to one-third of their level in NPCs.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ENO2, a known neuron-specific gene, increased by ~two fold during neuronal differentiation.
source: An exception was ENO2, a known neuron-specific gene, which increased by ~two fold.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: GLUT1/3 and HK2 expression dropped ~ten fold during neuronal differentiation.
source: GLUT1/3 and HK2, encoding glucose transporters and hexokinase, respectively, dropped ~ten fold.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: TCA genes remained at the same level during neuronal differentiation.
source: In contrast to a general decrease in glycolysis genes, TCA genes remained at the same level during differentiation; an exception was isocitrate dehydrogenase, IDH2, the mitochondrial isoform of IDH, which dropped nearly 50% (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH2) dropped nearly 50% during neuronal differentiation.
source: In contrast to a general decrease in glycolysis genes, TCA genes remained at the same level during differentiation; an exception was isocitrate dehydrogenase, IDH2, the mitochondrial isoform of IDH, which dropped nearly 50% (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Expression of the genes encoding the subunits of PDC itself showed no significant changes during neuronal differentiation.
source: Expression of the genes encoding the subunits of PDC itself, including PDHA1, PDHB, PDHX, DLAT, and DLD, showed no significant changes (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: RNA levels of PDK1, PDK3, and PDK4 declined significantly during neuronal differentiation.
source: Except for PDK2, RNA levels of the other three PDKs declined significantly during neuronal differentiation; in contrast, PDP1 RNA levels increased ~2.5 fold at 3 weeks of differentiation (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: PDP1 RNA levels increased ~2.5 fold at 3 weeks of differentiation.
source: Except for PDK2, RNA levels of the other three PDKs declined significantly during neuronal differentiation; in contrast, PDP1 RNA levels increased ~2.5 fold at 3 weeks of differentiation (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The overall changes in PDC kinase and phosphatase levels would favor increased PDC complex activity in neurons.
source: The overall changes in PDC kinase and phosphatase levels would favor increased PDC complex activity in neurons, and indeed PDH Ser300 phosphorylation, a major inhibitory site, decreased considerably during neuronal differentiation consistent with an increase in PDC activity (see Figure 3A).
evidence: Inferred from changes in PDK and PDP levels, and supported by data showing decreased PDH Ser300 phosphorylation.

claim: PDH Ser300 phosphorylation decreased considerably during neuronal differentiation.
source: The overall changes in PDC kinase and phosphatase levels would favor increased PDC complex activity in neurons, and indeed PDH Ser300 phosphorylation, a major inhibitory site, decreased considerably during neuronal differentiation consistent with an increase in PDC activity (see Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The levels of 3-phosphoglyerate (3PG) in neurons dropped to ~52% of those in NPCs.
source: Consistent with the overall decreased gene expression in glycolysis and glucose transporters, the levels of 3-phosphoglyerate (3PG) and pyruvate in neurons dropped to ~52% and 32% of those in NPCs.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolite analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The levels of pyruvate in neurons dropped to 32% of those in NPCs.
source: Consistent with the overall decreased gene expression in glycolysis and glucose transporters, the levels of 3-phosphoglyerate (3PG) and pyruvate in neurons dropped to ~52% and 32% of those in NPCs.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolite analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The levels of TCA intermediates in neurons were lower than those in NPCs.
source: The levels of TCA intermediates in neurons were also lower than those in NPCs: citrate was ~32% of that in NPCs, α-ketoglutarate was ~17%, fumarate was ~30%, and malate was ~22%; succinate was relatively higher, at ~62%, which may be due to the decreased protein level of SDHB in complex II, which catalyzes the conversion from succinate to fumarate (see Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolite analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The basal and maximum OCRs of 3-week differentiated neurons were significantly higher than in NPCs.
source: The basal and maximum OCRs of NPCs were ~82 and 130 (pmoles/min/10 µg), whereas those in 3-week differentiated neurons were ~98 and 183, significantly higher than in NPCs, consistent with increased TCA cycle flux.
evidence: Supported by Seahorse extracellular flux analyzer data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: The lactate production/glucose consumption ratio was ~1.61 for NPCs and ~0.35 for neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7, the ratio was ~1.61 lactate/glucose for NPCs, while in neurons, it was ~0.35, consistent with a significant decrease in aerobic glycolysis in neurons.
evidence: Supported by lactate and glucose measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: NPCs mainly expressed PKM2, whereas neurons expressed PKM1.
source: NPCs mainly expressed PKM2, whereas neurons expressed PKM1, as confirmed by RT-PCR with isoform-specific primers (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Primary human astrocytes only expressed PKM2.
source: In contrast, primary human astrocytes only expressed PKM2.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mouse neurons exclusively expressed PKM1, whereas astrocytes only expressed PKM2.
source: This result was consistent with a recent finding that mouse neurons exclusively expressed PKM1, whereas astrocytes only expressed PKM2 (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited reference and RNA-seq data from mouse cells shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The splicing shift from PKM2 to PKM1 occurred during neuronal differentiation from NPCs.
source: Our results established that the splicing shift from PKM2 to PKM1 occurred during neuronal differentiation from NPCs.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data comparing NPCs and neurons.

claim: hnRNPI, hnRNPA1 and hnRNPA2 RNA levels decreased to nearly 40% during neuronal differentiation.
source: Consistent with this model, during neuronal differentiation, hnRNPI, hnRNPA1 and hnRNPA2 RNA levels decreased to nearly 40% compared to NPCs (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: OGDH in NPCs (OGDH1) uses exon 4, whereas the isoform in neurons (OGDHneu) uses two adjacent exons.
source: OGDH in NPCs (OGDH1) uses exon 4, whereas the isoform in neurons, here called OGDHneu, uses two adjacent exons (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The alternative splicing of OGDH was confirmed by RT-PCR with isoform-specific primers.
source: The alternative splicing of OGDH was confirmed by RT-PCR with isoform-specific primers (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Primary human astrocytes only expressed OGDH1.
source: Primary human astrocytes also only expressed OGDH1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OGDHneu splicing is conserved in mouse neurons.
source: OGDHneu splicing is conserved in mouse neurons, whereas mouse astrocytes, like human astrocytes, only expressed OGDH1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from mouse cells shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A stretch of 34 amino acids in OGDH1, containing a Ca2+-binding motif, is replaced by 45 amino acids specific to OGDHneu.
source: As a result of this splice switch, a stretch of 34 amino acids in OGDH1, containing a Ca2+-binding motif (Armstrong et al., 2014), is replaced by 45 amino acids specific to OGDHneu (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 2E and cited reference.

claim: The OGDHneu isoform (LS1) is insensitive to Ca2+.
source: In a recent study, Denton et al. (2016) also detected this splice form of OGDH in the whole brain tissue and pancreatic islets, calling it LS1, and, importantly, they confirmed that LS1 isoform is insensitive to Ca2+.
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: HK2 and LDHA proteins almost completely disappeared upon neuronal differentiation.
source: HK2 and LDHA mRNAs were about 15% and 25% of those in NPCs, but strikingly, both proteins almost completely disappeared upon differentiation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HK2 and LDHA could readily be detected in NPCs but not in neurons by immunostaining.
source: Consistent with the immunoblotting data, HK2 and LDHA could readily be detected in NPCs but not in neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The levels of citrate synthase (CS), isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH2) and succinyl-CoA ligase β subunit (SUCLA2) were constant during differentiation.
source: For the TCA enzymes, the levels of citrate synthase (CS), isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH2) and succinyl-CoA ligase β subunit (SUCLA2) were constant during differentiation (Figure 3A), even though IDH2 showed ~50% decrease at the RNA level.
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The disappearance of LDHA is a major switch for downregulating aerobic glycolysis as NPCs differentiate.
source: Thus, it appears that the disappearance of LDHA is, mechanistically, a major switch for downregulating aerobic glycolysis as NPCs differentiate, allowing a transition into a neuronal mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation state.
evidence: Inferred from the dramatic decrease in LDHA and its role in aerobic glycolysis.

claim: Depletion of HK2 or LDHA significantly slowed the propagation of NPCs by 2.6~3.5 fold.
source: Depletion of HK2 or LDHA significantly slowed the propagation of NPCs by 2.6~3.5 fold (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Aerobic glycolysis is required for NPC proliferation.
source: These results indicate that, as found in cancer cell lines (Fantin et al., 2006; Wolf et al., 2011), aerobic glycolysis is required for NPC proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from knockdown experiments and supported by cited references.

claim: Both c-MYC and N-MYC could bind to the HK2 and LDHA promoters in human NPCs.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, chromatin immunopreciptation with anti-c-MYC and N-MYC antibodies in human NPCs showed that both MYCs could bind to the HK2 and LDHA promoters in the region containing the E boxes as reported (Kim et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 3F and cited reference.

claim: Overexpression of c-MYC upregulated HK2 and LDHA expression in NPCs.
source: Consistently, we found that overexpression of c-MYC using a doxycycline-inducible lentivirus upregulated HK2 and LDHA expression in NPCs (Figure 3F), indicating that MYC controls HK2 and LDHA expression in these cells similarly to other types of cells previously studied.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Both c-MYC and N-MYC protein levels decreased significantly once NPCs differentiated into neurons.
source: Both c-MYC and N-MYC protein levels decreased significantly, by ~70% and ~85% respectively, once NPCs differentiated into neurons (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The decreased expression of HK2 and LDHA during neuronal differentiation was most likely attributable predominantly to the observed MYC decrease.
source: Therefore, the decreased expression of HK2 and LDHA during neuronal differentiation was most likely attributable predominantly to the observed MYC decrease occurring as NPCs exited from the cell cycle and entered the differentiation process.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between MYC decrease and HK2/LDHA decrease, and the known role of MYC in regulating these genes.

claim: LDHA was downregulated in neurons directly converted from fibroblasts using Ngn2 and Ascl1 overexpression.
source: The second protocol using Ngn2 and Ascl1 overexpression generated more iNs, and the Tuj1-positive neurons did not have an LDHA immunofluorescence signal (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: LDHA was also downregulated in neurons directly converted from fibroblasts, indicating a metabolic resetting during transdifferentiation.
source: These data established that LDHA was also downregulated in neurons directly converted from fibroblasts, indicating a metabolic resetting during transdifferentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LDHA is downregulated in both NPC-derived neurons and directly converted neurons.

claim: Three-week neuronal cultures differentiated from NPCs constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA showed a significant fraction of GFAP-positive glial cells (~40% of total cells).
source: Three-week neuronal cultures differentiated from NPCs constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA showed a significant fraction of GFAP-positive glial cells, ~40% of total cells, compared to only ~4% GFAP-positive cells in neuronal cultures from control vector-transduced NPCs.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neuronal cultures from NPCs constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA had ~40% condensed nuclei, compared to ~6% in control.
source: The neuronal cultures from NPCs constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA had ~40% condensed nuclei, an indicator of apoptotic cells, which was much higher than control, ~6%, and such increased cell death was not observed in NPCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by nuclear staining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: AMPK pT172 was clearly increased at day 4 of neuronal differentiation in cultures constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA compared to control.
source: Indeed, AMPK pT172 was clearly increased at day 4 of neuronal differentiation compared to control, but the phosphorylation returned to a level comparable to control at day 21, when extensive cell death had already occurred (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Day-4 neuronal cultures constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA showed ~four fold increase of lactate secretion compared to control cultures.
source: Day-4 neuronal cultures constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA showed ~four fold increase of lactate secretion compared to control cultures (Figure 4J), indicating increased aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: Supported by lactate measurement data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Increasing the level of pyruvate in neuronal differentiation medium rescued the neuronal death caused by HK2 and LDHA expression.
source: If the neuronal death were due to excessive conversion of pyruvate to lactate resulting in reduced pyruvate entry into mitochondria, increasing the level of pyruvate in neuronal differentiation medium might be able to rescue the neuronal death. This was indeed the case; as shown in Figure 4K, coexpression of LDHA and MAP2 was readily detected in cells grown in differentiation medium containing 5 mM sodium pyruvate, ten-fold higher than the standard concentration (0.5 mM), and there was no irregular punctate staining of LDHA as seen with standard neuronal differentiation medium (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: After the first week of neuronal differentiation, the neuronal mtDNA copy number doubled compared to NPCs.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, after the first week, the neuronal mtDNA copy number doubled compared to NPCs, and at 3 weeks was increased to ~four fold.
evidence: Supported by mtDNA copy number measurement data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At 3 weeks of neuronal differentiation, mtDNA copy number was increased to ~four fold compared to NPCs.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, after the first week, the neuronal mtDNA copy number doubled compared to NPCs, and at 3 weeks was increased to ~four fold.
evidence: Supported by mtDNA copy number measurement data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 3-week differentiated neurons contained ~four-fold higher protein mass than NPCs.
source: Consistent with neurons being larger cells than NPCs, we found that 3-week differentiated neurons contained ~four-fold higher protein mass than NPCs (Figure 5B), similar to the increase in mtDNA copy number.
evidence: Supported by protein mass measurement data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No significant difference in mitochondrial respiratory complex protein levels was found between NPCs and neurons at 1 and 3 weeks, except for SDHB of complex II.
source: When the amounts of mitochondrial respiratory complexes were examined by immunoblotting with equal protein loading of cell lysates, no significant difference was found between NPCs and neurons at 1 and 3 weeks, except for SDHB of complex II, which was consistently ~50% lower in neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mitochondrial density remains largely unchanged during neuronal differentiation.
source: It appears that although mitochondrial mass increases on a per cell basis, mitochondrial density remains largely unchanged during neuronal differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mitochondrial protein levels per unit protein are similar between NPCs and neurons.

claim: PGC-1α levels were significantly increased during neuronal differentiation (~three fold increase at 1 week and ~four fold at 3 week).
source: We went on to analyze the expression profiles of transcription factors involved in mitochondrial biogenesis: PGC-1α levels were significantly increased, ~three fold increase at 1 week and ~four fold at 3 week; ERRγ levels were also upregulated, ~2.8 fold at 1 week and ~3.4 at 3 week, and similar changes were observed in their protein levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ERRγ levels were upregulated during neuronal differentiation (~2.8 fold at 1 week and ~3.4 at 3 week).
source: We went on to analyze the expression profiles of transcription factors involved in mitochondrial biogenesis: PGC-1α levels were significantly increased, ~three fold increase at 1 week and ~four fold at 3 week; ERRγ levels were also upregulated, ~2.8 fold at 1 week and ~3.4 at 3 week, and similar changes were observed in their protein levels (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The expression of the majority of the genes encoding mitochondrial respiratory complexes was either slightly decreased or unchanged in neurons.
source: Surprisingly, despite the significant increases in PGC-1α and ERRγ, the expression of the majority of the genes encoding mitochondrial respiratory complexes was either slightly decreased or unchanged in neurons (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PGC-1α was required to maintain the levels of ENO1 and PKM in glycolysis.
source: We found that PGC-1α was required to maintain the levels of ENO1 and PKM in glycolysis; CS, ACO2, OGDH and SUCLA2 in TCA cycle; TFAM and TFBM1 in mtDNA replication and transcription, and NRF1 (nuclear respiratory factor-1), a key transcription factor that activates nuclear genes encoding respiratory complex subunits (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PGC-1α was required to maintain the levels of CS, ACO2, OGDH and SUCLA2 in TCA cycle.
source: We found that PGC-1α was required to maintain the levels of ENO1 and PKM in glycolysis; CS, ACO2, OGDH and SUCLA2 in TCA cycle; TFAM and TFBM1 in mtDNA replication and transcription, and NRF1 (nuclear respiratory factor-1), a key transcription factor that activates nuclear genes encoding respiratory complex subunits (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PGC-1α was required to maintain the levels of TFAM and TFBM1 in mtDNA replication and transcription.
source: We found that PGC-1α was required to maintain the levels of ENO1 and PKM in glycolysis; CS, ACO2, OGDH and SUCLA2 in TCA cycle; TFAM and TFBM1 in mtDNA replication and transcription, and NRF1 (nuclear respiratory factor-1), a key transcription factor that activates nuclear genes encoding respiratory complex subunits (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Almost all the representative genes for each mitochondrial respiratory complex exhibited decreased expression in PGC-1α knockdown neurons.
source: Consistently, almost all the representative genes for each mitochondrial respiratory complex exhibited decreased expression in PGC-1α knockdown neurons (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ERRγ was mainly required for maintaining expression of NRF1 and mitochondrial respiratory complexes.
source: In contrast to the broad effect of PGC-1α, ERRγ was mainly required for maintaining expression of NRF1 and mitochondrial respiratory complexes (Figure 5F), which is consistent with a recent finding that in neurons the genomic binding sites for ERRγ have extensive overlap with NRFs (Pei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by knockdown experiment data shown in Figure 5F and cited reference.

claim: The increased expression of PGC-1α/ERRγ during neuronal differentiation appears to maintain, rather than increase, the transcription of metabolic and mitochondrial genes as in NPCs.
source: Therefore, the increased expression of PGC-1α/ERRγ during neuronal differentiation appears to maintain, rather than increase as assumed, the transcription of metabolic and mitochondrial genes as in NPCs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that metabolic gene expression levels remain unchanged despite increased PGC-1α/ERRγ, and knockdown experiments showing these factors are required to maintain expression.

claim: There is distinct transcriptional control of metabolic and mitochondrial OXPHOS genes in proliferating versus post-mitotic differentiated cells.
source: This observation also implies that there is distinct transcriptional control of metabolic and mitochondrial OXPHOS genes in proliferating versus post-mitotic differentiated cells as discussed below.
evidence: Inferred from the shift in transcriptional regulators from MYC/E2F in NPCs to PGC-1α/ERRγ in neurons.

claim: Downregulation of LDHA is a key switch for turning off aerobic glycolysis during neuronal differentiation.
source: First, downregulation of LDHA is a key switch for turning off aerobic glycolysis.
evidence: Inferred from the dramatic decrease in LDHA and its role in converting pyruvate to lactate.

claim: The absence of LDHA in neurons is consistent with previous immunohistochemistry studies in human brain showing that neurons are exclusively stained with anti-LDHB antibody while astrocytes are stained by both anti-LDHA and LDHB antibodies.
source: The absence of LDHA in neurons is consistent with previous immunohistochemistry studies in human brain showing that neurons are exclusively stained with anti-LDHB antibody while astrocytes are stained by both anti-LDHA and LDHB antibodies (Bittar et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: The shift of pyruvate kinase from PKM2 to PKM1 by alternative mRNA splicing is likely to be important for the metabolic transition.
source: Second, the shift of pyruvate kinase from PKM2 to PKM1 by alternative mRNA splicing is likely to be important.
evidence: Inferred from the observed splicing shift and known differences in PKM1 and PKM2 activity.

claim: The decreased expression of HK2, and the GLUT1 and GLUT3 glucose transporters reduce glucose entry, terminating high flux glycolysis.
source: Third, the decreased expression of HK2, and the GLUT1 and GLUT3 glucose transporters reduce glucose entry, terminating high flux glycolysis.
evidence: Inferred from the observed decreases in HK2 and glucose transporter expression.

claim: The decrease in expression of PDKs and the increase in PDPs may result in more active pyruvate dehydrogenase complexes (PDC).
source: Fourth, the decrease in expression of PDKs and the increase in PDPs may result in more active pyruvate dehydrogenase complexes (PDC), as demonstrated by decreased phosphorylation at Ser 300 of PDH E1 alpha protein (PDHA1), promoting pyruvate entry into the TCA cycle.
evidence: Inferred from changes in PDK and PDP expression and supported by decreased PDH phosphorylation data.

claim: A need to avoid aerobic glycolysis is the major reason underlying neuronal reliance on oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Thus, it appears that a need to avoid aerobic glycolysis is the major reason underlying neuronal reliance on oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that neurons shut down aerobic glycolysis but do not increase TCA/OXPHOS gene expression.

claim: UCP2 expression levels dropped significantly during neuronal differentiation, and in 3-week neurons the UCP2 level was only 20% of that in NPCs.
source: We found that during neuronal differentiation, UCP2 expression levels dropped significantly, and in 3-week neurons the UCP2 level was only 20% of that in NPCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating that similar mitochondrial metabolism remodeling occurs in neurons.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Turning off aerobic glycolysis allows the efficient use of pyruvate for energy production.
source: Therefore, turning off aerobic glycolysis allows the efficient use of pyruvate for energy production.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that constitutive HK2/LDHA expression causes neuronal death that can be rescued by extra pyruvate.

claim: Lactate secreted by glial cells is a critical energy source for neurons in vivo.
source: Many lines of evidence support the conclusion that lactate secreted by glial cells is a critical energy source for neurons in vivo (Pellerin and Magistretti, 2012), and blocking neuronal oxidative utilization of lactate affects neuronal survival and even memory formation (Suzuki et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Downregulation of LDHA would favor the reverse reaction, which is catalyzed by a tetramer composed of LDHB to generate pyruvate from exogenous lactate.
source: Obviously, downregulation of LDHA, an enzyme catalyzing the conversion of pyruvate to lactate, would favor the reverse reaction, which is catalyzed by a tetramer composed of LDHB to generate pyruvate from exogenous lactate.
evidence: Inferred from the known enzymatic properties of LDHA and LDHB.

claim: Exposure of NPCs to hypoxia leads to more glial cells during neuronal differentiation.
source: Interestingly, it has been reported that exposure of NPCs to hypoxia, which boosts aerobic glycolysis, leads to more glial cells during neuronal differentiation (Xie et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: During neuronal differentiation, the transcriptional control of mitochondrial genes and metabolic genes shifts from a cell-cycle mode to a post-mitotic neuronal program.
source: It appears that, during neuronal differentiation, the transcriptional control of mitochondrial genes and metabolic genes shifts from a cell-cycle mode to a post-mitotic neuronal program: in proliferating NPCs, MYC and E2Fs activate the transcription of metabolic genes, while in differentiated neurons, PGC-1α and ERRγ are responsible (Figure 5G).
evidence: Inferred from the observed changes in transcriptional regulators and their effects on metabolic gene expression.

claim: In proliferating NPCs, MYC and E2Fs activate the transcription of metabolic genes.
source: It appears that, during neuronal differentiation, the transcriptional control of mitochondrial genes and metabolic genes shifts from a cell-cycle mode to a post-mitotic neuronal program: in proliferating NPCs, MYC and E2Fs activate the transcription of metabolic genes, while in differentiated neurons, PGC-1α and ERRγ are responsible (Figure 5G).
evidence: Inferred from the high expression of MYC and E2Fs in NPCs and their known roles in metabolic gene regulation.

claim: In differentiated neurons, PGC-1α and ERRγ are responsible for the transcription of metabolic genes.
source: It appears that, during neuronal differentiation, the transcriptional control of mitochondrial genes and metabolic genes shifts from a cell-cycle mode to a post-mitotic neuronal program: in proliferating NPCs, MYC and E2Fs activate the transcription of metabolic genes, while in differentiated neurons, PGC-1α and ERRγ are responsible (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by knockdown experiments showing PGC-1α and ERRγ are required to maintain metabolic gene expression in neurons.

claim: OGDH has a novel and conserved neuronal splicing shift, resulting in the loss of a calcium binding motif.
source: In addition, OGDH, a key enzyme in the TCA cycle, has a novel and conserved neuronal splicing shift, resulting in the loss of a calcium binding motif.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing the splicing shift and sequence analysis showing loss of the calcium binding motif.

claim: Neural progenitor cells (NPCs) are less reliant on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production than are non-dividing differentiated neurons.
source: A pioneering study using embryonic Xenopus retina revealed that neural progenitor cells (NPCs) are less reliant on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production than are non-dividing differentiated neurons, and the transition from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation is tightly coupled to neuronal differentiation, though the exact molecular basis underlying the transition is unknown (Agathocleous et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: The transition from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation is tightly coupled to neuronal differentiation.
source: A pioneering study using embryonic Xenopus retina revealed that neural progenitor cells (NPCs) are less reliant on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP production than are non-dividing differentiated neurons, and the transition from glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation is tightly coupled to neuronal differentiation, though the exact molecular basis underlying the transition is unknown (Agathocleous et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: PGC-1α knockout mice show obvious neurodegenerative pathology.
source: PGC-1α may also play a key role in neuronal metabolism, as PGC-1α knockout mice show obvious neurodegenerative pathology (Lin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Deletion of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) impairs maintenance and proliferation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
source: For instance, deletion of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) impairs maintenance and proliferation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Most cancer cells use aerobic glycolysis to generate energy, a phenomenon called the Warburg effect.
source: Most cancer cells use aerobic glycolysis to generate energy, a phenomenon called the Warburg effect, in which a large fraction of glycolytic pyruvate is converted into lactate (Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by cited reference.

claim: Only high-quality NPC lines containing more than 90% Sox2 and Nestin double-positive cells were used for experiments.
source: Only high-quality NPC lines containing more than 90% Sox2 and Nestin double-positive cells were used for experiments.
evidence: Methodological criterion stated in the text.

claim: Glial cells emerged and proliferated after 4–5 weeks of neuronal differentiation.
source: Although rare at 3 weeks, glial cells emerged and proliferated after 4–5 weeks; therefore, 3-week neuronal cultures were used to represent a population of developing neurons.
evidence: Observational data from the differentiation experiments.

claim: The top 200 up-regulated genes during neuronal differentiation were enriched in neuronal function pathways, including synapse formation, transmission of nerve impulses, gated channel activity and neuronal projections.
source: Most of the down-regulated genes were cell cycle related, whereas up-regulated genes were enriched in neuronal function pathways, including synapse formation, transmission of nerve impulses, gated channel activity and neuronal projections (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Most of the down-regulated genes during neuronal differentiation were cell cycle related.
source: Most of the down-regulated genes were cell cycle related, whereas up-regulated genes were enriched in neuronal function pathways, including synapse formation, transmission of nerve impulses, gated channel activity and neuronal projections (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Neuron-specific genes such as NEUROD2, MYT1L, MAPT (Tau), SYN1 (synapsin), CHD5 were significantly increased during neuronal differentiation.
source: Neuron-specific genes such as NEUROD2, MYT1L, MAPT (Tau), SYN1 (synapsin), CHD5 (Egan et al., 2013) were significantly increased (Figure 1E), whereas the markers associated with proliferating NPCs, LIN28A/B and FOXM1 (Cimadamore et al., 2013; Karsten et al., 2003), were considerably decreased (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E and cited reference.

claim: The markers associated with proliferating NPCs, LIN28A/B and FOXM1, were considerably decreased during neuronal differentiation.
source: Neuron-specific genes such as NEUROD2, MYT1L, MAPT (Tau), SYN1 (synapsin), CHD5 (Egan et al., 2013) were significantly increased (Figure 1E), whereas the markers associated with proliferating NPCs, LIN28A/B and FOXM1 (Cimadamore et al., 2013; Karsten et al., 2003), were considerably decreased (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1F and cited references.

claim: For a majority of the glycolytic reactions, only a single enzyme was predominantly expressed in NPCs or neurons.
source: For most of the glycolytic reactions, there are multiple paralogous enzymes, but according to our RNA-seq data, for a majority of the reactions only a single enzyme was predominantly expressed in NPCs or neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: HK1 exhibited minor increases during neuronal differentiation.
source: Notably, HK1, the other hexokinase, and PFKM, a phosphofructokinase, functioning at the first two irreversible steps of glycolysis, exhibited minor increases.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: PFKM exhibited minor increases during neuronal differentiation.
source: Notably, HK1, the other hexokinase, and PFKM, a phosphofructokinase, functioning at the first two irreversible steps of glycolysis, exhibited minor increases.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The genes at the beginning steps of the pentose phosphate pathway involved in NADPH production showed unchanged expression levels during differentiation.
source: Overall, the genes at the beginning steps involved in NADPH production showed unchanged expression levels during differentiation, but the levels of the ones on the branch required for nucleotide synthesis decreased, consistent with neuronal post-mitotic status (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The levels of pentose phosphate pathway genes on the branch required for nucleotide synthesis decreased during neuronal differentiation.
source: Overall, the genes at the beginning steps involved in NADPH production showed unchanged expression levels during differentiation, but the levels of the ones on the branch required for nucleotide synthesis decreased, consistent with neuronal post-mitotic status (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Absolute metabolite levels do not directly reflect true metabolite flux.
source: It should be noted that absolute metabolite levels do not directly reflect true metabolite flux, i.e., the observed reduction in TCA cycle intermediates does not necessarily mean that carbon flux through the TCA cycle is decreased.
evidence: General principle of metabolic biochemistry.

claim: PKM1 is normally found in tissues where oxidative phosphorylation is preferentially used to generate ATP.
source: PKM1 is normally found in tissues where oxidative phosphorylation is preferentially used to generate ATP, whereas PKM2 is expressed in proliferating cells with high anabolic activity (Imamura and Tanaka, 1972).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by cited reference.

claim: PKM2 is expressed in proliferating cells with high anabolic activity.
source: PKM1 is normally found in tissues where oxidative phosphorylation is preferentially used to generate ATP, whereas PKM2 is expressed in proliferating cells with high anabolic activity (Imamura and Tanaka, 1972).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by cited reference.

claim: PKM1 is constitutively active, while PKM2 is subjected to allosteric regulation and can adopt a low or high activity state.
source: PKM1 is constitutively active, while, PKM2 is subjected to allosteric regulation and can adopt a low or high activity state (Anastasiou et al., 2012).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by cited reference.

claim: Replacing PKM2 with PKM1 in cancer cells reduces lactate production and increases oxygen consumption.
source: Replacing PKM2 with PKM1 in cancer cells reduces lactate production and increases oxygen consumption (Christofk et al., 2008), indicating that PKM2 may favor high flux glycolysis.
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: PKM1 expression does not affect upstream glycolytic intermediates but significantly reduces nucleotide biosynthesis.
source: A recent study reveals that PKM1 expression does not affect upstream glycolytic intermediates but significantly reduces nucleotide biosynthesis (Lunt et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: PKM splicing or the PKM2/PKM1 ratio is controlled by the expression levels of hnRNPI, hnRNPA1 and hnRNPA2.
source: PKM splicing or the PKM2/PKM1 ratio is known to be controlled by the expression levels of nuclear ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP) proteins, hnRNPI, hnRNPA1 and hnRNPA2, and in cancer cells, these proteins are expressed at high levels and bind repressively to the sequences flanking exon 9, favoring the exon 10 addition thus generating more PKM2 (David et al., 2010; Clower et al., 2010).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by cited references.

claim: OGDH encodes the E1 subunit of the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, catalyzing the conversion of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA in the TCA cycle.
source: OGDH encodes the E1 subunit of the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, catalyzing the conversion of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA in the TCA cycle.
evidence: Established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Mitochondrial calcium increases can boost OGDH activity.
source: Mitochondrial calcium increases can further boost its activity (Denton, 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: There was still considerable expression of OGDH1 in neurons.
source: Different from the more exclusive PKM splicing, there was still considerable expression of OGDH1 in neurons.
evidence: Observed from RNA-seq data.

claim: The OGDHneu isoform was not found in RNA-seq data from cardiomyocytes.
source: Note, that we did not find the OGDHneu isoform in RNA-seq data from cardiomyocytes, indicating that, unlike PKM1, OGDHneu is not specific for cells that preferentially use oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: Observational data from RNA-seq analysis.

claim: OGDH neuron-specific splicing may avoid a prolonged activation of the OGDH complex as a result of frequent intracellular calcium increases.
source: Calcium is used in a variety of neuronal functions. We suspect that OGDH neuron-specific splicing may avoid a prolonged activation of the OGDH complex as a result of frequent intracellular calcium increases.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the loss of calcium binding motif and neuronal calcium dynamics.

claim: The loss of HK2 and LDHA expression during neuronal differentiation is conserved in mouse cells.
source: To explore if the loss of HK2 and LDHA expression during neuronal differentiation is conserved, we checked HK2 and LDHA expression during differentiation of mouse neuroprogenitor cells derived from embryonic stem cell. As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, both HK2 and LDHA mRNA levels dropped, falling to ~8.5% and ~11% of the level in NPCs, respectively, and, consistently, their protein levels were also greatly decreased.
evidence: Supported by data from mouse cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sustained levels of HK1 mRNA and protein were observed during mouse neuronal differentiation.
source: In contrast, as in human cells, sustained levels of HK1 mRNA and protein, were observed during mouse neuronal differentiation.
evidence: Supported by data from mouse cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inhibitory effect of HK2 depletion on NPC proliferation is consistent with a recent finding that ablation of HK2 diminishes aerobic glycolysis and disrupts cerebellar granule neuronal progenitor development.
source: The inhibitory effect of HK2 depletion on NPC proliferation is consistent with a recent finding that ablation of HK2 diminishes aerobic glycolysis and disrupts cerebellar granule neuronal progenitor development (Gershon et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: MYC directly activates HK2 and LDHA transcription.
source: MYC, a key transcription factor associated with cell cycle progression, directly activates HK2 and LDHA transcription, and the promoter regions of HK2 and LDHA contain MYC binding sites (5'-CACGTG-3'), also known as E box (Kim et al., 2004).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by cited reference.

claim: MYC promotes a high PKM2/PKM1 ratio by upregulating heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNP) that regulate PKM alternative splicing.
source: MYC also promotes a high PKM2/PKM1 ratio by upregulating heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNP) that regulate PKM alternative splicing (David et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: c-MYC and N-MYC redundantly promote neural progenitor cell proliferation in the developing brain.
source: c-MYC and N-MYC redundantly promote neural progenitor cell proliferation in the developing brain, with the brains of double knockout mice exhibiting profoundly impaired growth (Wey and Knoepfler, 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Dox-induced expression of c-Myc is sufficient to re-activate HK2 expression in neurons.
source: Dox-induced expression of c-Myc is sufficient to re-activate HK2 expression in neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Functional induced neurons (iN) can be generated directly from fibroblasts by forced expression of neural specific transcription factors.
source: Functional induced neurons (iN) can be generated directly from fibroblasts by forced expression of neural specific transcription factors, a process also called transdifferentiation (Vierbuchen et al., 2010).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by cited reference.

claim: PTB KD iNs were not as mature as Ngn2/Ascl1-derived iNs.
source: Furthermore, while Ngn2/Ascl1-derived iNs expressed Tau, a mature neuronal marker, no Tau expression was detected in iNs from PTB knockdown, suggesting that PTB KD iNs were not as mature as Ngn2/Ascl1-derived iNs (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Neurons cannot tolerate constitutive HK2 and LDHA expression and die during differentiation.
source: The results suggest that neurons cannot tolerate constitutive HK2 and LDHA expression and die during differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased neuronal death when HK2 and LDHA are constitutively expressed.

claim: Neurons detected in the culture differentiated from NPCs constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA may have been derived from the fraction of NPCs not expressing HK2 and LDHA.
source: Neurons detected in the culture differentiated from NPCs constitutively expressing HK2 and LDHA may have been derived from the fraction of NPCs not expressing HK2 and LDHA.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation that not all NPCs expressed the transgenes.

claim: A likely reason for the neuronal death is mitochondrial ATP production deficiency.
source: As aerobic glycolysis diverts pyruvate from mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation for energy production by converting it into secreted lactate, a likely reason for the neuronal death is mitochondrial ATP production deficiency.
evidence: Inferred from the role of aerobic glycolysis in diverting pyruvate from mitochondria.

claim: Turning off aerobic glycolysis is critical to maintain the normal neuronal ATP level.
source: These results imply that turning off aerobic glycolysis is critical to maintain the normal neuronal ATP level.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased AMPK phosphorylation and neuronal death when aerobic glycolysis is maintained.

claim: A transcriptional circuit, including PGC-1 family coactivators, estrogen-related receptors (ERRs) and nuclear respiratory factor (NRF), is responsible for the transcription of metabolic and mitochondrial genes in multiple tissues.
source: A transcriptional circuit, including PGC-1 family coactivators, estrogen-related receptors (ERRs) and nuclear respiratory factor (NRF), is responsible for the transcription of metabolic and mitochondrial genes in multiple tissues, such as heart and skeletal muscle (Scarpulla et al., 2012).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge supported by cited reference.

claim: PGC-1α is induced in the neonatal mouse heart concurrent with the increase of mitochondrial energy-producing capacity.
source: PGC-1α is induced in the neonatal mouse heart concurrent with the increase of mitochondrial energy-producing capacity (Lehman et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: PGC-1α not only stimulates the induction of NRF1, but also binds to and coactivates the transcriptional function of NRF1 in muscle cells.
source: PGC-1α not only stimulates the induction of NRF1, but also binds to and coactivates the transcriptional function of NRF1 in muscle cells (Wu et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: In neurons the genomic binding sites for ERRγ have extensive overlap with NRFs.
source: In contrast to the broad effect of PGC-1α, ERRγ was mainly required for maintaining expression of NRF1 and mitochondrial respiratory complexes (Figure 5F), which is consistent with a recent finding that in neurons the genomic binding sites for ERRγ have extensive overlap with NRFs (Pei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: c-MYC-null fibroblasts have diminished mitochondrial mass.
source: c-MYC-null fibroblasts have diminished mitochondrial mass (Li et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: c-MYC activation in the myocardium of adult mice induces mitochondrial biogenesis and glycolysis but reduces PGC-1α level.
source: c-MYC activation in the myocardium of adult mice induces mitochondrial biogenesis and glycolysis but reduces PGC-1α level (Ahuja et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: E2F upregulates mitochondrial genes, a function conserved from flies to mammals.
source: E2F also upregulates mitochondrial genes, a function conserved from flies to mammals (Ambrus et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: In a high-throughput screen to identify small molecules interfering with mitochondrial abundance, hundreds of compounds were found to be capable of changing the cellular mitochondrial content; the majority of them also change cell size accordingly.
source: Interestingly in this regard, in a high-throughput screen to identify small molecules interfering with mitochondrial abundance, hundreds of compounds were found to be capable of changing the cellular mitochondrial content; the majority of them also change cell size accordingly (Kitami et al., 2012), indicating a fundamental relationship between cell size and mitochondrial number.
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: There is a fundamental relationship between cell size and mitochondrial number.
source: Interestingly in this regard, in a high-throughput screen to identify small molecules interfering with mitochondrial abundance, hundreds of compounds were found to be capable of changing the cellular mitochondrial content; the majority of them also change cell size accordingly (Kitami et al., 2012), indicating a fundamental relationship between cell size and mitochondrial number.
evidence: Inferred from cited reference showing correlation between mitochondrial content and cell size.
